title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 70
paragraphs: These, then, perished thus ingloriously. Meanwhile the Persians and the rest of the throng, having fled for refuge to the palisade, succeeded in getting up onto the towers before the Lacedaemonians came up; and once up, they reinforced the defensive wall as best they could. When the Lacedaemonians came up to attack it, a vigorous fight for the wall began between them. As long as the Athenians were away, they defended themselves and had much the advantage over the Lacedaemonians, who did not understand the art of fighting against walls; but when the Athenians came up to help, then there was a fierce fight for the wall lasting a long time, and at last, by valor and endurance, the Athenians mounted the wall and made a breach, through which the Greeks poured in. The Tegeans were the first to enter the wall, and they plundered Mardonius's tent, taking, besides the other things in it, the manger of his horse, which was all of bronze and a sight worth seeing. This manger of Mardonius was dedicated by the Tegeans as an offering in the temple of Athena Alea; but everything else they took, they brought to the common stock of the Greeks. The barbarians, once the wall was captured, no longer formed themselves into any close body, nor did any of them think of making a stand, but they were utterly at a loss, as you would expect from men in a panic with many tens of thousands shut up in a small space; and the Greeks were able to slaughter them, so that out of an army of three hundred thousand — subtracting the forty thousand Artabazos took with him in his flight — of the remainder not three thousand men survived. Of the Lacedaemonians from Sparta, ninety-one were killed in battle; of the Tegeans, sixteen; and of the Athenians, fifty-two.
